title: Guarding the Fundamental Mind
author: Zhanran
excerpt: After seeing the nature, never forgetting to guard the fundamental mind at all times is of utmost importance — this is the work of sustaining and preserving. The Essentials of Mind Cultivation says: “Those who awaken to this (the fundamental mind) and guard it abide in the one-suchness and are liberated without stirring; those who are deluded about it and turn their backs on it go to the six realms (six paths) and revolve in birth and death for long kalpas.” (See A Detailed Explanation of the Essentials of Mind Cultivation.)

inline.s: After seeing the nature, never forgetting to guard the fundamental mind at all times is of utmost importance — this is the work of sustaining and preserving.
The Essentials of Mind Cultivation says:
“Those who awaken to this
(the fundamental mind)
and guard it abide in the one-suchness and are liberated without stirring; those who are deluded about it and turn their backs on it go to the six realms
(six paths)
and revolve in birth and death for long kalpas.”
(For details, see
A Detailed Explanation of the Essentials of Mind Cultivation
[The fundamental mind]
The fundamental mind is empty, still, and free of thought, without defilement, so it is also called the pure mind. It is without knowing and yet knows all, so it is also called the
mind of spiritual awareness

. Note that the “knowing” of spiritual awareness is a knowing that grasps no appearances; to distinguish it from the appearance-grasping knowing of seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition, it is called spiritual awareness. The Record of the Mirror of the Source says:
“Prajñā's non-knowing means having no knowing that grasps appearances.”
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says:
“To establish knowing within seeing and knowing is the root of ignorance; seeing and knowing without any view — this is nirvāṇa, flawless and truly pure.”

Practice is to still this scattered consciousness-mind (the mind of discrimination and deliberation) and thereby reach the state of the fundamental mind (the mind of spiritual awareness) — as it is said,
“When the mad mind does not rest, its very resting is bodhi.”
The Essentials of Mind Transmission says:
“When thoughts are stilled and
(wang, “forgotten”)
deliberations cease, the Buddha appears of himself.”
The Buddha Repository Sutra says:
“The anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas is without thought and without mentation.”

Practice is to return to the root and source, transforming the state of the consciousness-mind (the mind that discriminates by clinging to the six sense-objects) into the state of the fundamental mind (the empty, still mind of spiritual awareness). Awakening is awakening to this empty, still, spiritually-aware mind; cultivation is guarding this empty, still, spiritually-aware mind. First preserve, then allow natural functioning, until reaching non-doing.
[Abiding in the one-suchness] “Abiding” means to hold firmly.
“One-suchness”:

“One” means non-duality; “suchness” means non-difference. Non-dual and non-different is called one-suchness. “Abiding in the one-suchness” means holding firmly to the one-suchness. In concrete practice, it means: do not think over good or evil, grasp no appearances, and remain unmoving in suchness. The Sixth Patriarch said:

“If you wish to know the essentials of the mind, simply do not think over any good or evil at all; you will naturally enter the pure mind-essence, deeply clear and eternally still, with wondrous functions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges
(wondrous functions endless as the Ganges' sands)
(See
A Detailed Explanation of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch
.) [Sustaining and preserving]
After awakening (seeing the nature),

cultivation has two stages — preserving and allowing: First, preserving: protect one's own mind and do not run after states, in order to subdue afflictions. Second, allowing: let the mind function naturally and do not run after states, in order to cut off afflictions. [Allowing natural functioning] Letting the mind operate naturally of itself.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra
, “The Manifestation of the Tathāgata” chapter, says:
“There is no living being who does not possess the Tathāgata's wisdom; it is only because of deluded thoughts and inverted attachment that they do not realize it.
If they depart from deluded thoughts
, the all-knowing wisdom, the natural wisdom, and the unobstructed wisdom will appear before them.”
If they depart from deluded thoughts

This has three levels: the cessation of coarse thoughts, the cessation of subtle thoughts, and even the cessation of the most subtle thoughts. For example, for one who recites the Buddha's name, deluded thoughts are coarse thoughts, while the thought of reciting the Buddha's name is a subtle thought. Usually, when both coarse and subtle thoughts have ceased, this is called no-thought — the no-thought generally spoken of. Going further, if the most subtle thoughts also come to rest, this is the ultimate no-thought. Therefore, the meaning of the word “no-thought” must be determined from the context. [The most subtle thought] The subtle arising-and-ceasing flux of the consciousness-mind, which is the characteristic of the ālaya consciousness. The Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna says:
“As when a bodhisattva reaches the end of the stages
(has completed the ten stages)
, perfecting his skillful means, in a single thought he corresponds to the initial arising of the enlightened mind, and the mind has no initial characteristic;
because he has distanced himself from the most subtle thoughts,
he sees the mind-nature,
and the mind abides forever,
which is called ultimate enlightenment
Master Guifeng said:
“If the subtle flux
(the most subtle thoughts)

all becomes still, and only the great wisdom of perfect enlightenment shines alone, then, according to circumstances, one manifests hundreds of thousands of millions of bodies to deliver beings with whom one has affinity,
and this is called Buddha
(See The Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp)

[The all-knowing wisdom] Being able to know and understand all inner dharmas and inner names, and also to know and understand all outer dharmas and outer names. [The natural wisdom] The wisdom that arises naturally, without contrived effort. [The unobstructed wisdom] The wisdom that is free and unobstructed — namely, the wisdom of the Buddha.
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says:
“All living beings, from time without beginning, continue in birth and death, all because they do not know the permanently abiding true mind, the essence of pure and luminous nature
(all because they do not know how to abide in the true mind, this essence of pure and luminous nature)
, and instead employ deluded thoughts
(and so employ deluded thoughts)
; these thoughts are unreal, and so there is revolving.”

[The true mind, the essence of pure and luminous nature] The essence of pure and luminous nature is the luminous, wondrous essence that is by nature pure. Grammatically, “the essence of pure and luminous nature” is an appositive modifying the noun “true mind.” [Revolving] Rebirth with physical segments and rebirth through transformation. [Rebirth with physical segments] Beings in the three realms and six paths, elicited by good and evil karma, have lifespans that are limited and bodies that differ in kind, so their birth and death is called “rebirth with physical segments.” Those who end rebirth with physical segments escape the cycle of transmigration. [Rebirth through transformation] Sages of the three vehicles, having cut off the delusions of views and thoughts and ended rebirth with physical segments, in the course of cultivating the Way gradually extinguish delusion and gradually increase realization. This migration between delusion and awakening differs in each period; the shift from an earlier period to a later one is just like a round of birth and death, but its transformation is wondrous, unfathomable, and inconceivable, so it is called “rebirth through transformation.” Those who end rebirth through transformation perfectly realize the fruit of Buddhahood.
Question: How does one awaken to this and guard it?
Answer: It is as the Essentials of Mind Cultivation
says:
“Therefore, after awakening, one must long
observe and examine
, and when deluded thoughts suddenly arise, never follow them. Reduce and reduce again, until reaching non-doing
(at this stage of non-doing, one need not observe and examine, for thoughts arise but are not followed)
; only then is it ultimate. This is what all good spiritual friends of the world
call “herding the ox after awakening”
The Blue Cliff Record records:
Mazu was walking with his disciple Baizhang when they saw wild ducks fly by. The Master said: What is that? Baizhang said: Wild ducks. The Master said: Where have they gone
(testing whether Baizhang abides in form and gives rise to mind)
? Baizhang said: They have flown past. The Master thereupon twisted Baizhang's nose; Baizhang cried out in pain. The Master said:
When did they ever fly away!
Baizhang had an awakening at these words
(xǐng: Baizhang woke up at these words)

Baizhang's first answer, “Wild ducks,” was like a mirror reflecting things, and this was correct; but his second answer, “They have flown past,” was abiding in form and giving rise to mind — following states and chasing things, failing to guard the fundamental mind (losing right mindfulness). So Mazu twisted his nose, wanting him to turn back and guard the fundamental mind. In the midst of the pain, Baizhang heard his teacher say: When did they ever fly away? (Wild ducks are illusory — how could there be coming or going?) and he suddenly awakened:
“One should give rise to the pure mind in this way.”
(By twisting Baizhang's nose, Mazu wanted him
never to forget to guard the fundamental mind at all times
, and not to follow states and chase after things.)

[Baizhang] The Chan master Huaihai, called the Great-Wisdom Master of Mount Baizhang in Hongzhou of the Tang, dharma-heir of Chan Master Mazu Daoyi. He was the first to establish the rules of the Chan community, the so-called “Baizhang Pure Rules.” [When did they ever fly away] Gathering the appearances back into the nature, and merging them into emptiness.
[Gathering appearances back into the nature] Dissolving the myriad phenomena into the true reality of all dharmas, seeing only the unborn within the apparent arising and ceasing. (For details, see
The True Reality of All Dharmas
All that has appearance is illusory.”

If one does not depart from appearances, it is hard to realize the Way; so Mazu, with the thunderbolt means that give no time to cover one's ears, struck Baizhang's unawakened mind. The Vajrasamādhi Sūtra says:
“The dharma of ‘if you lose the fundamental mind, you should at once repent’ is what brings coolness.”
From this, the conduct of a strict teacher and a worthy disciple can be seen in part, letting us intimately feel that “the fragrance of plum blossoms comes from the bitter cold.”
The Compendium of the Five Lamps says:
“The master
(Baizhang)

was attending Mazu on a walk when a flock of wild ducks flew by. Mazu said: ‘What is that?’ The master said: ‘Wild ducks.’ Mazu said: ‘Where are they going?’ The master said: ‘They have flown away.’ Mazu then twisted the master's nose; he cried out in pain. Mazu said: ‘And you still say they flew away!’ At these words the master had an awakening. He returned to the attendants' quarters and wept bitterly. A colleague asked: ‘Are you remembering your parents, ye
(an ancient form of “ye”)

?’ The master said: ‘No.’ ‘Were you scolded by someone?’ The master said: ‘No.’ ‘Then why are you crying?’ The master said: ‘My nostrils were twisted by the great master and the pain is unbearable.’ The colleague said: ‘Is there some matter in which you do not see eye to eye?’ The master said: ‘Go ask the abbot.’ The colleague asked the great master: ‘What matter is it that Attendant Hai does not see eye to eye, that he weeps in the quarters? Please tell me, for the sake of
(me)
.’ The great master said: ‘
He
(he)
understands
(has realized)

Ask him yourself.’ The colleague returned to the quarters and said: ‘The abbot says you understand, and told me to ask you myself.’ The master then laughed heartily. The colleague said: ‘Just now you were weeping; why are you laughing now?’ The master said: ‘Just now I wept; now I laugh.’ The colleague was baffled. The next day, Mazu ascended the hall. The assembly had just gathered when the master came out and rolled up the mat
(the prostrating mat)

. Mazu then descended from the seat, and the master followed him to the abbot's room. Mazu said: ‘Just now I had not said a word; why did you roll up the mat?’ The master said: ‘Yesterday the abbot twisted my nose and it hurt.’ Mazu said: ‘Where were you attending yesterday?’ The master said: ‘The nose does not hurt today.’ Mazu said: ‘
You have deeply understood yesterday's matter.
’ The master bowed and withdrew.”
Question: What was Baizhang weeping so bitterly about? And what was he laughing so heartily about?

Answer: What he wept so bitterly about was this: from beginningless kalpas, simply because he did not know to “gather appearances back into the nature and guard the fundamental mind,” he had suffered torments all in vain and sunk in confusion until now. What he laughed so heartily about was this: now that he had received this wondrous dharma, if he would only strive and practice earnestly, he would surely attain the true fruit in this very life. What a boundless joy — at last he could return to the source of all things! Truly it is: Cultivation has no other cultivation, it lies only in recognizing the road; when the road is recognized, birth and death are both brought to rest.
The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch records:
One day he thought: The time has come to spread the Dharma; I can no longer stay hidden
(an ancient form of “retreat”)

. So he came out, and arrived at the Faxing Temple in Guangzhou, where Master Yinzong was lecturing on the Nirvāṇa Sūtra. At that time the wind was blowing and a banner was fluttering; one monk said: The wind is moving. Another monk said: The banner is moving. The debate went on endlessly. Huineng stepped forward and said: It is not the wind that moves, nor the banner that moves, it is
your minds, kind sirs, that move
. The whole assembly was astounded.

Translation: One day I (the Sixth Patriarch Huineng) thought to myself: the time is ripe, and now I should spread the Dharma; I can no longer hide forever in the mountains and forests. So I came out of the mountains and arrived at the Faxing Temple in Guangzhou, where I found Master Yinzong lecturing on the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra. At that moment the wind was moving a banner; one monk said: It is the wind moving the banner. Another monk said: It is the banner moving of itself. They argued without end. I stepped forward and said: It is not the wind that moves, nor the banner that moves of itself; it is your two minds that move (
you have failed to guard the fundamental mind
). Hearing this, the crowd was greatly astonished.

[Master Yinzong] A native of Wu Commandery (Wu County, Jiangsu). He left home to become a monk under a teacher and was deeply versed in the Nirvāṇa Sūtra. In the first year of the Xianheng reign of the Tang, he arrived at the capital and was ordered by imperial decree to reside at the Dajing'ai Temple. He firmly declined and went to Qichun to pay respects to Master Hongren (the Fifth Patriarch of Chan). Later, at the Faxing Temple in Guangzhou, while lecturing on the Nirvāṇa Sūtra, he met the Sixth Patriarch, Master Huineng, and only then awakened to the profound principle; he took Huineng as his master of dharma transmission. He also gathered the words of accomplished ones from the Liang to the Tang and composed The Collection of the Essentials of the Mind, which circulated widely. On the twenty-first day of the second month of the second year of the Xiantian reign, he passed away at the Miaoxi Temple on Mount Kuaiji, at the age of eighty-seven. [Banner] A long strip of flag hung straight, hoisted on a bamboo pole or the like. [Kind sir] A Buddhist term of respect in addressing others. The original meaning of “kind sir” is a person of virtue, or a person who has shown kindness. [The whole assembly] The crowd.

[It is not the wind that moves, nor the banner that moves; it is your minds that move] The wind moving and the banner moving are matters within the dream of ignorance. For worldly people to argue about whether the wind moves or the banner moves is not altogether blameworthy, for they are sunk in the dream of ignorance; but practitioners must awaken from the dream of ignorance, and so should firmly grasp that “all that has appearance is illusory,” and “do not give rise to mind abiding in form, do not give rise to mind abiding in sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharma,”
guarding the fundamental mind
and not being turned by states, and only thus can they end birth and death. In the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, the Buddha says:

“You should all know that all living beings, from time without beginning, continue in birth and death, all because they do not know the permanently abiding true mind, the essence of pure and luminous nature
(all because they do not know how to abide in the true mind, this essence of pure and luminous nature)
, and instead employ deluded thoughts
(and so employ deluded thoughts)
; these thoughts are unreal, and so there is revolving.”

So these two monks were arguing about whether the wind moved or the banner moved; this is clinging to appearances as real, letting the mind be turned by states, and employing deluded thoughts — truly not the conduct of practitioners. “It is not the wind that moves, nor the banner that moves” says, from the viewpoint of awakening (gathering appearances back into the nature), that “all that has appearance is illusory,” “originally there is not a single thing” — how could there be any moving of wind or banner? And the phrase “it is your minds that move” goes to the very root:
“Because the mind arises, all kinds of dharmas arise; because the mind ceases, all kinds of dharmas cease.”
(The Sūtra of Divining Good and Evil Karmic Retribution) Master Hanshan said:
“All dharmas have differences only in reliance on deluded thoughts. Apart from the mind's thoughts, there are no characteristics of any realm at all.”

(Hanshan's Notes on the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra) [Because the mind arises, all kinds of dharmas arise; because the mind ceases, all kinds of dharmas cease] “Because the mind arises, all kinds of dharmas arise” means that when the mind arises (the first stirring of thought) one enters the dream of ignorance, and so all kinds of dharmas appear; “because the mind ceases, all kinds of dharmas cease” means that when the mind ceases (the most subtle thought ceases) and the dream of ignorance awakens, then all the dharmas seen in the dream cease.

Huineng thus settled the debate from the root, which shows how lofty his state was (by “lofty state” is meant not some abstruse words or wondrous phrases, but the real skill of remaining unmoving in suchness when the sense-roots meet their objects); hence “the whole assembly was astounded.” The phrase “It is not the wind that moves, nor the banner that moves; it is your minds that move” is truly earth-shattering! Living beings, within the deeply clear unborn, see only arising and ceasing; the Buddhas, within the apparent arising and ceasing, see only the unborn.
The Sixth Patriarch Huineng was originally an illiterate wood-seller of Nanhai. Seeing a guest reciting a sutra, the moment he heard the words,
“One should give rise to the mind without abiding anywhere,”
his mind opened in awakening. Traveling for over thirty days, he arrived at Huangmei (the East Chan Temple in Huangmei County, Hubei) and bowed to the Fifth Patriarch, then said:
“This disciple's own mind constantly gives rise to wisdom; not departing from the self-nature is itself the field of blessings.”
[Nanhai] A commandery name, belonging to the Yuehai circuit of Guangdong.

During the thirty-odd days of seeking the Dharma and the eight-odd months of splitting firewood and pounding rice, Huineng worked with painful effort on this very passage of scripture; in less than ten months he attained great awakening and succeeded to the patriarchate.
(See
A Detailed Explanation of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch
[This passage of scripture] The Diamond Sūtra says:

“All bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas should give rise to the pure mind in this way: they should not give rise to mind abiding in form, they should not give rise to mind abiding in sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharma; they should give rise to the mind without abiding anywhere.”

We living beings, from beginningless kalpas, have revolved through the six paths and suffered torments, all because we give rise to mind by clinging to appearances — and the appearances we cling to are illusory! What a boundless injustice! So the Diamond Sūtra makes the truth plain, dispelling our inverted thoughts of a billion kalpas. [They should not give rise to mind abiding in form, they should not give rise to mind abiding in sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharma; they should give rise to the mind without abiding anywhere] One should not cling to the sense-object realms (the objects of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharma) and give rise to the mind of discrimination and deliberation (the mind that discriminates, calculates, loves, hates, chooses, and rejects); one should give rise, without any abiding or attachment, to the pure mind (the mind undefiled by the sense-object realms).
See
A Detailed Explanation of the Diamond Sūtra
for details.
The Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna says:
“Trusting in one's own nature, knowing that the mind stirs deludedly and that there are no present objects,
practice the dharma of distancing

. Because one truly knows there are no present objects, by various skillful means one engages in practice that accords, neither grasping nor thinking, until after a long time, through the power of habituation, ignorance is extinguished. Because ignorance is extinguished, the mind no longer arises. Because it does not arise, objects cease accordingly. Because both causes and conditions have ceased, mind and characteristics are all exhausted; this is called attaining nirvāṇa and accomplishing natural karmic (wisdom).”

Translation: Deeply trust that your own nature is Buddha, know that this is the mind stirring deludedly, and that there are in fact no present objects; then practice the dharma of distancing (“Knowing it is illusory, one departs at once, with no further skillful means; departing from the illusion, one is at once awakened, with no gradual stages”). Because one truly knows there are no present objects, by various skillful means one engages in practice that accords, neither grasping nor thinking, until after a long time, through the power of habituation, ignorance is extinguished. Because ignorance is extinguished, the mind no longer arises. Because the mind does not arise, objects cease accordingly. Because both causes and conditions have ceased, the mind (the mind of discrimination and deliberation) and characteristics all perish; this is called attaining nirvāṇa and accomplishing natural karmic wisdom.

[No present objects] There are no objects before one. The appearance of objects is an illusion produced by the mind's deluded stirring. [Habituation] “Perfuming” means to fumigate and bring forth; “habit” means doing something repeatedly over a long time until it becomes instinct (habit becoming second nature). Continually grasping at defiled or pure conditions fumigates and brings forth the mind-essence into defilement or purity, and so it is called habituation. Ignorance is the cause of defiled fumigation; brightness is the cause of pure fumigation. Giving rise to deluded views is ignorance; departing from deluded views is brightness. [Both causes and conditions cease] The mind's deluded stirring is the cause of objects appearing; and objects appearing in turn become the aiding condition for the mind's deluded stirring, making the mind stir even more. Cause and condition reinforce each other, growing ever more intense. “Both causes and conditions cease” means the mind no longer stirs deludedly, and objects also cease. [Natural karmic wisdom] This is the subsequently attained wisdom. [Subsequently attained wisdom] One of the two wisdoms. When object and wisdom are undifferentiated and no discrimination arises, it is called the “fundamental wisdom”; when one discriminates the characteristics of all differences with clear luminous insight, it is called the “subsequently attained wisdom.”
